{"task": {"question": "An image has an absolute 25 MiB allowance for the complete required installation. Among MicaX and R7, which can be accepted without removing required components?", "options": ["MicaX", "R7"]}, "context": "x01s2 | Archive transfer package and storage inspection
The branch image builder also recorded the installation sizes of the packages with their required libraries. Required installed footprints are 46 MiB for Tide-4 4.2, 29 MiB for MicaX 6, and 83 MiB for R7 7.1. These are uncompressed sizes on the branch system volume. Optional graphical consoles were removed before measurement; removing any remaining library made the package fail its startup check. A compressed download can be smaller, but that number does not describe the space the package occupies while operating. Installation instructions should therefore quote installed footprint when space on a branch image is the constraint.

x01s1 | Branch archive transfer: transport qualification memo
The transport rig used one worker, eight thousand files, a 512 MiB process allowance, and a link that alternated between ninety seconds available and four minutes unavailable. The test retained the process between outages, and a separate test killed it after a chunk write. Under the alternating-link test, Tide-4 resumed all transfers without sending previously acknowledged chunks again. Under the same alternating-link test, MicaX restarted the current file after every outage and could not resume acknowledged chunks. R7 resumed all acknowledged chunks under the alternating-link test. File contents were checked against the sealed manifest after the final acknowledgement. Duplicate network frames were permitted, but rewriting a chunk that the server had already acknowledged was counted as a failed resume.

x01s3 | Branch archive adoption worksheet and unresolved measurements
The adoption worksheet collects operational details that were not part of the transport rig. All three clients can be launched from a scheduled job and can read a manifest without an interactive desktop. Tide-4 exposes a machine-readable checkpoint counter. MicaX provides a final report for each file but no checkpoint counter. R7 exposes both a checkpoint counter and a staging-directory inventory. The inventory helps operators account for space occupied by unfinished transfers; it is not itself a proof that a transfer can safely resume.

x01s3 | Branch archive adoption worksheet and unresolved measurements
The current packet contains no measured peak resident memory for Tide-4, MicaX, or R7 on any ARM processor. A desktop demonstration showed all three running on an x86 workstation, but the demonstration did not sample resident memory. The 512 MiB allowance on the transport rig was a process limit, not an observed peak, and it did not establish whether any client could operate below 128 MiB. Engineers should avoid translating an allowance into a measurement. Likewise, total machine memory displayed by the operating system includes unrelated services and cannot be assigned to the transfer client.

x01s3 | Branch archive adoption worksheet and unresolved measurements
A small branch image should be sized using the required installed footprints from the storage inspection. Free space required for user inputs is additional. The team has not authorized deleting the original input after a local checksum, because only central acknowledgement proves that another recoverable copy exists. A proposed low-space workflow would keep large source files on removable media, but none of the qualification runs used removable media. Its performance, disconnect behavior, and failure recovery remain separate questions from the ordinary system-volume setup.

x01s1 | Branch archive transfer: transport qualification memo
The rig measured file completion and network work, not every deployment concern. It did not simulate credential revocation or a clock moving backward. Operators must retain the original files until central acknowledgement, even when the client has displayed a complete local checksum pass. The engineering team considers that retention rule a workflow requirement common to all three methods rather than a differentiating feature."}

{"task": {"question": "A different deployment requires a measured p95 forwarding latency at most 10 ms while using 256-bit encryption mode. Which candidate can be approved from the measurements in this packet?", "options": ["Kestrel", "R3", "Nacre-10"]}, "context": "x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
Encryption coverage is limited. No 256-bit encryption-mode latency test was performed for Kestrel, R3, or Nacre-10. The main interruption and electrical runs used encryption disabled. A short installation demonstration enabled a 128-bit profile on all three devices and confirmed that a stream appeared, but it did not record latency percentiles. Neither result establishes p95 forwarding latency in the 256-bit mode. The proposed follow-up includes key loading, steady traffic, and rekeying, but its draft procedure has no observations in this packet.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
The verification replay reports that Kestrel firmware 2.2 did not isolate the secondary port within 240 ms under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile. Worksheet A and the replay describe the same Kestrel configuration and loop event, and both remain active with no reconciliation or precedence rule. The replay observed a warning at 75 ms while forwarding continued, which explains why an alarm-only check might appear encouraging. However, neither report defines the required event as an alarm. The packet contains no accepted correction identifying an instrumentation error or a different cable map.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
For ordinary operations, all three bridges expose a local status page that can be viewed without an external account. Kestrel and Nacre-10 export packet counters with timestamps; R3 exports cumulative counts and a last-reset time. These interfaces can help a maintenance team identify a changed link, but they do not resolve the contradictory loop-isolation records or supply an absent encrypted-latency measurement. The team plans to retain raw receiver traces with future reports so ordering and response time can be recomputed independently. That planned improvement is an evidence-management step, not a new performance result for any of the currently evaluated bridges.

x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
Under the active two-uplink ordinary profile, measured DC input power was 5.4 W for Kestrel firmware 2.2, 4.8 W for R3 firmware 3.3, and 8.2 W for Nacre-10 firmware 10.1. These results include the bridges' own wired transceivers. No external camera power is supplied by the bridges. A standby reading for Nacre-10 was lower, but standby disables the stream and cannot establish its operating power during active aggregation. The current deployment worksheet asks about measured active power rather than adapter size.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
The camera-network group compared Kestrel bridge firmware 2.2, R3 bridge firmware 3.3, and Nacre-10 bridge firmware 10.1. Each bridge has two wired uplinks connected through the same laboratory link emulator. The ordinary profile carries one ordered camera stream with encryption disabled. Packets include sequence numbers so the receiver can identify loss, duplicates, and arrival-order changes. This packet uses each method name for the complete bridge hardware and stated firmware, not for a generic aggregation algorithm that might appear in another device.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
A second exploratory trace contained small telemetry messages rather than camera packets. R3 showed no reordering there, but that trace had a different packet schedule and is not a replacement for the ordinary camera-stream result. All three bridges emitted a local link-state event when A disappeared. The event can support an operator alert but does not prove ordering at the receiver; the packet sequence check supplies that evidence. The report recommends keeping failure recovery, stream ordering, electrical consumption, and unrelated wiring-fault behavior as distinct measured properties when specifying a deployment."}

Which tested configuration fits that budget?", "options": ["F3", "Lantern-P", "Wisp8"]}, "context": "x03s2 | Logger energy budget and operator recovery review
At twenty degrees Celsius with the specified ten-second schedule, daily board energy was 0.84 Wh for F3, 1.12 Wh for Lantern-P, and 0.68 Wh for Wisp8. Those figures include scheduled storage flushes. An earlier spreadsheet omitted a periodic metadata flush and is not reproduced here; this review uses the corrected full-day captures. The packet has no corresponding cold-temperature energy measurement. Selecting a logger on a room-temperature budget therefore means applying the stated room-temperature criterion, not claiming that cold battery life has been established.

x03s2 | Logger energy budget and operator recovery review
Energy measurements used the same F3, Lantern-P, and Wisp8 configurations as chamber qualification. The bench supply logged current continuously over a full day at twenty degrees Celsius, with the sensor simulator requesting one measurement every ten seconds. The measured quantity is energy consumed by the entire logger board, including its regulator and storage. Radio transmission was disabled because the target shelter uses a wired service visit. Battery chemistry and self-discharge are excluded; the results describe load consumption and do not directly predict months of unattended service.

x03s1 | Remote logger chamber qualification
The field-device group tested three logger configurations for an unheated instrument shelter. F3 is firmware 3.6 on board F; Lantern-P is firmware 2.1 on board L; Wisp8 is firmware 8.0 on board W. Each board carries the same sensor simulator and records one signed measurement every ten seconds. The simulator independently records the generated sequence numbers, allowing the team to count missing measurements after a run. All reported temperature results concern the complete board and firmware combination, not firmware in isolation.

x03s2 | Logger energy budget and operator recovery review
The operator recovery exercise removed power during a metadata write on each board while the service cable was absent. F3 firmware 3.6 recovered its log automatically at the next boot, with no service tool required. Lantern-P firmware 2.1 required the proprietary service tool to unlock its log after an interrupted metadata write. Wisp8 firmware 8.0 recovered automatically at the next boot. Every board preserved already sealed measurements during the exercise, but accessibility differed: preserved data behind an operator lock is not automatically available to a visit team. The shelter visit kit intentionally contains a generic serial terminal and no vendor-specific recovery application.

x03s2 | Logger energy budget and operator recovery review
A proposed workaround for Lantern-P would keep a service tool permanently attached inside the shelter. The team has not measured its energy draw or tested unattended recovery with that arrangement. It would also introduce another board into the environmental qualification scope. The review records the proposal to help future engineering, while keeping it outside the evidence for the tested standalone logger configurations. Maintenance frequency, battery replacement logistics, and connector durability remain planning considerations, but none can remove an explicit requirement to recover using only the equipment the visit team actually carries.

x03s1 | Remote logger chamber qualification
At minus 25 degrees Celsius for forty-eight hours, F3 recorded every scheduled measurement and its maximum wake-to-record latency was 180 ms. At minus 25 degrees Celsius for forty-eight hours, Lantern-P recorded every scheduled measurement and its maximum wake-to-record latency was 140 ms. At minus 25 degrees Celsius for forty-eight hours, Wisp8 missed seventeen scheduled measurements after a clock stall. A room-temperature Wisp8 run had no missing measurements and a maximum latency of 95 ms. No external controller participated in these rollback runs. JettyS and Umbra-2 used the writable data volume with a read-only root; C4 used a writable root as required by its activation registry. x05s3 | Rollback timing and isolation boundary review
The review also recorded recovery details that may matter for a future trial. JettyS retains a bounded local history of image changes. C4 keeps only the current and previous activation entries. Umbra-2 can retain several image generations subject to data-volume space. History length is not a guarantee of rollback compatibility, because application state can evolve independently of an image identifier. Operators should test the actual state transition they intend to reverse. For this packet, the supported timing claim is deliberately limited to compatible state, a retained image, and the local command path measured in the exercise.

x05s3 | Rollback timing and isolation boundary review
Rollback testing began with the new service already running and a previous service image retained on the data volume. The operator issued a local rollback command without contacting an external controller. Application state was intentionally kept compatible with both images, since a deployment manager cannot generally undo an arbitrary database migration. The reported interval ends when the previous image passes the service's ordinary readiness probe. C4's shorter interval should be considered alongside its early termination behavior; it is not a like-for-like advantage for a workload that requires draining every accepted transaction. A stateless preview application might make a different choice because its requests can be retried without operational loss.

x05s2 | Deployment manager filesystem and package audit
All managers can accept preloaded images through a local command without contacting a remote orchestrator. The audit disconnected the network and used a local operator account for these commands. This establishes the observed operation path; it does not claim that an appliance needs no network for its actual inspection workload. The team also checked that logs can be exported from the data volume after a reboot. Permission repair, image signing policy, and management of operator accounts belong to the surrounding appliance image and are not automatically supplied by any of these three managers."}

The S80 workload joins sales records to account metadata and groups the result by region. One account owns eighty percent of the sales records. On S80 with the standard rule pack, CedarPlan-6 used 3.6 GiB peak workspace and finished in 74 seconds. On S80 with the standard rule pack, Vela used 2.4 GiB peak workspace and finished in 69 seconds. Its required response is automatic isolation of the secondary port; reporting a warning without isolation does not count. Worksheet A reports that Kestrel firmware 2.2 isolated the secondary port in 82 ms under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile. Under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile, R3 firmware 3.3 isolated the secondary port in 160 ms, and Nacre-10 firmware 10.1 did so in 140 ms. Timing starts when the loop is physically closed.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
The guard verification technician recreated topology LG-4 from worksheet A and confirmed the Kestrel firmware 2.2 image, ordinary-profile checksum, port assignments, emulator firmware, and cable map. The same single-loop event was applied at the documented connection point. Timing used the same physical closure trigger. The observation distinguishes an alarm from actual port isolation by measuring forwarding at the secondary port, so a visible warning light alone cannot satisfy the stated loop-guard response.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
The verification replay reports that Kestrel firmware 2.2 did not isolate the secondary port within 240 ms under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile. Worksheet A and the replay describe the same Kestrel configuration and loop event, and both remain active with no reconciliation or precedence rule. The replay observed a warning at 75 ms while forwarding continued, which explains why an alarm-only check might appear encouraging. However, neither report defines the required event as an alarm. The packet contains no accepted correction identifying an instrumentation error or a different cable map.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
For ordinary operations, all three bridges expose a local status page that can be viewed without an external account. Kestrel and Nacre-10 export packet counters with timestamps; R3 exports cumulative counts and a last-reset time. These interfaces can help a maintenance team identify a changed link, but they do not resolve the contradictory loop-isolation records or supply an absent encrypted-latency measurement. The team plans to retain raw receiver traces with future reports so ordering and response time can be recomputed independently. That planned improvement is an evidence-management step, not a new performance result for any of the currently evaluated bridges.

x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
Under the active two-uplink ordinary profile, measured DC input power was 5.4 W for Kestrel firmware 2.2, 4.8 W for R3 firmware 3.3, and 8.2 W for Nacre-10 firmware 10.1. These results include the bridges' own wired transceivers. No external camera power is supplied by the bridges. A standby reading for Nacre-10 was lower, but standby disables the stream and cannot establish its operating power during active aggregation. The current deployment worksheet asks about measured active power rather than adapter size.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
The interruption procedure removes uplink A while uplink B remains available and records the time until delivery resumes through B. In the ordinary-profile uplink-A interruption test, Kestrel resumed through B in 42 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets. In the same test, R3 resumed through B in 31 ms but delivered twenty-three out-of-order packets. Nacre-10 resumed through B in 64 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets in that test. The receiver lacked a reorder buffer, so out-of-order arrivals are operationally relevant even when every payload byte eventually arrives."}

{"task": {"question": "Under the documented LG-4 single-loop event with the ordinary profile, the secondary port must be automatically isolated within 100 ms. A warning alone is insufficient. Can any evaluated bridge be selected on a resolved evidentiary basis?", "options": ["Kestrel", "R3", "Nacre-10"]}, "context": "x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
The loop-guard exercise deliberately miswires the downstream test lead to create the single-loop topology documented as LG-4. Its required response is automatic isolation of the secondary port; reporting a warning without isolation does not count. Worksheet A reports that Kestrel firmware 2.2 isolated the secondary port in 82 ms under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile. Under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile, R3 firmware 3.3 isolated the secondary port in 160 ms, and Nacre-10 firmware 10.1 did so in 140 ms. Timing starts when the loop is physically closed.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
The guard verification technician recreated topology LG-4 from worksheet A and confirmed the Kestrel firmware 2.2 image, ordinary-profile checksum, port assignments, emulator firmware, and cable map. The same single-loop event was applied at the documented connection point. Timing used the same physical closure trigger. The observation distinguishes an alarm from actual port isolation by measuring forwarding at the secondary port, so a visible warning light alone cannot satisfy the stated loop-guard response.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
The verification replay reports that Kestrel firmware 2.2 did not isolate the secondary port within 240 ms under topology LG-4 with the ordinary profile. Worksheet A and the replay describe the same Kestrel configuration and loop event, and both remain active with no reconciliation or precedence rule. The replay observed a warning at 75 ms while forwarding continued, which explains why an alarm-only check might appear encouraging. However, neither report defines the required event as an alarm. The packet contains no accepted correction identifying an instrumentation error or a different cable map.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
For ordinary operations, all three bridges expose a local status page that can be viewed without an external account. Kestrel and Nacre-10 export packet counters with timestamps; R3 exports cumulative counts and a last-reset time. These interfaces can help a maintenance team identify a changed link, but they do not resolve the contradictory loop-isolation records or supply an absent encrypted-latency measurement. The team plans to retain raw receiver traces with future reports so ordering and response time can be recomputed independently. That planned improvement is an evidence-management step, not a new performance result for any of the currently evaluated bridges.

x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
Under the active two-uplink ordinary profile, measured DC input power was 5.4 W for Kestrel firmware 2.2, 4.8 W for R3 firmware 3.3, and 8.2 W for Nacre-10 firmware 10.1. These results include the bridges' own wired transceivers. No external camera power is supplied by the bridges. A standby reading for Nacre-10 was lower, but standby disables the stream and cannot establish its operating power during active aggregation. The current deployment worksheet asks about measured active power rather than adapter size.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
The interruption procedure removes uplink A while uplink B remains available and records the time until delivery resumes through B. In the ordinary-profile uplink-A interruption test, Kestrel resumed through B in 42 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets. In the same test, R3 resumed through B in 31 ms but delivered twenty-three out-of-order packets. Nacre-10 resumed through B in 64 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets in that test. The receiver lacked a reorder buffer, so out-of-order arrivals are operationally relevant even when every payload byte eventually arrives."}

Which candidate meets all three constraints?", "options": ["Kestrel", "R3", "Nacre-10"]}, "context": "x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
The interruption procedure removes uplink A while uplink B remains available and records the time until delivery resumes through B. In the ordinary-profile uplink-A interruption test, Kestrel resumed through B in 42 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets. In the same test, R3 resumed through B in 31 ms but delivered twenty-three out-of-order packets. Nacre-10 resumed through B in 64 ms and delivered zero out-of-order packets in that test. The receiver lacked a reorder buffer, so out-of-order arrivals are operationally relevant even when every payload byte eventually arrives.

x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
Under the active two-uplink ordinary profile, measured DC input power was 5.4 W for Kestrel firmware 2.2, 4.8 W for R3 firmware 3.3, and 8.2 W for Nacre-10 firmware 10.1. These results include the bridges' own wired transceivers. No external camera power is supplied by the bridges. A standby reading for Nacre-10 was lower, but standby disables the stream and cannot establish its operating power during active aggregation. The current deployment worksheet asks about measured active power rather than adapter size.

x08s2 | Bridge electrical measurements and loop-guard worksheet A
The electrical measurement uses the same complete bridges and ordinary unencrypted profile as interruption qualification. Both uplinks are connected, the reference camera stream is active, and the input supply is held at the nominal direct-current voltage. The meter records device input power rather than the rating printed on the supplied adapter. A rating is a maximum supply capability, whereas measured device power concerns the load under the stated operating condition. Cable losses outside the device input terminals are excluded.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
The camera-network group compared Kestrel bridge firmware 2.2, R3 bridge firmware 3.3, and Nacre-10 bridge firmware 10.1. Each bridge has two wired uplinks connected through the same laboratory link emulator. The ordinary profile carries one ordered camera stream with encryption disabled. Packets include sequence numbers so the receiver can identify loss, duplicates, and arrival-order changes. This packet uses each method name for the complete bridge hardware and stated firmware, not for a generic aggregation algorithm that might appear in another device.

x08s3 | Bridge guard replay and encryption-mode coverage
Encryption coverage is limited. No 256-bit encryption-mode latency test was performed for Kestrel, R3, or Nacre-10. The main interruption and electrical runs used encryption disabled. A short installation demonstration enabled a 128-bit profile on all three devices and confirmed that a stream appeared, but it did not record latency percentiles. Neither result establishes p95 forwarding latency in the 256-bit mode. The proposed follow-up includes key loading, steady traffic, and rekeying, but its draft procedure has no observations in this packet.

x08s1 | Dual-link bridge interruption laboratory record
A second exploratory trace contained small telemetry messages rather than camera packets. R3 showed no reordering there, but that trace had a different packet schedule and is not a replacement for the ordinary camera-stream result. All three bridges emitted a local link-state event when A disappeared. The event can support an operator alert but does not prove ordering at the receiver; the packet sequence check supplies that evidence. The report recommends keeping failure recovery, stream ordering, electrical consumption, and unrelated wiring-fault behavior as distinct measured properties when specifying a deployment."}

For Tide-4, all staging bytes remain encrypted on disk in release 4.2, including during resume and forced-exit recovery. Its in-memory checksum buffer is plaintext, so this statement should not be read as a guarantee about memory disclosure. MicaX 6 writes a plaintext compression spool on the system volume before uploading. R7 7.1 stages only ciphertext on disk, including after a forced exit. Deleting the original input file is outside the client contract: none of these packages automatically sanitizes files placed in the input directory by a user. The inspection treats those original inputs separately from client-created staging.

The 512 MiB allowance on the transport rig was a process limit, not an observed peak, and it did not establish whether any client could operate below 128 MiB. {"task": {"question": "An indefinitely disconnected parts kiosk considers only Larch and P6. It requires local index construction, changes, and queries plus byte-exact product-code equality that preserves case and punctuation, with no application post-filter. Which candidate meets those requirements?", "options": ["Larch", "P6"]}, "context": "x07s2 | Withdrawal visibility and product-code filter worksheet
The product-code exercise used literal codes that differ only in letter case and punctuation, alongside ordinary descriptive text. Larch build 4.1 provides byte-exact product-code equality filtering, preserving letter case and punctuation. P6 build 6.0 normalizes product-code filters by folding case and removing punctuation, merging distinct literal codes. Dune-15 build 15.2 also provides byte-exact product-code equality filtering. The supplied applications cannot add a post-filter because their stored results contain passage identifiers only; therefore the tested filter semantics must be supplied by the retrieval method itself.

x07s2 | Withdrawal visibility and product-code filter worksheet
These literal-code results do not imply anything about the quality of semantic matches for a paragraph-length question. The two functions have different purposes: descriptive queries can tolerate related wording, whereas an inventory code may designate another part when one character changes. The worksheet checked the exact filter field and did not disable normalization in the descriptive text index. No undocumented P6 flag for byte-exact filtering was evaluated. A future build might introduce a separate exact field, but the current build's documented product-code operation has the normalization behavior reported here.

x07s3 | Disconnected retrieval operations and index lifecycle review
Dune-15 build 15.2 and Larch build 4.1 can build, update, and query their local indices indefinitely without a network service or license refresh. P6 build 6.0 requires a remote calibration transaction after each thousand queries and refuses further queries if that transaction cannot complete. P6's initial query allowance let it appear operational early in the disconnected test, but it later stopped at the documented boundary. Preloading documents and vectors does not remove that dependency. There is no offline calibration package for build 6.0 in the inspected distribution.

x07s2 | Withdrawal visibility and product-code filter worksheet
The withdrawal exercise tested when a passage stops being eligible for retrieval. A client deletes a known passage identifier, waits for the deletion API acknowledgement, and immediately queries from a different client session. Both sessions connect to the same local service, with no replica or external cache between them. The test queries the withdrawn passage by a distinctive phrase and checks the returned identifiers. The acceptance boundary is the API acknowledgement, not the eventual completion of a background index cleanup.

x07s1 | Passage retrieval appliance performance record
All three can return stable passage identifiers suitable for linking into the original archive. That interface property is useful but does not establish that withdrawn material disappears at the required time. Nor does the performance run establish whether literal product-code filters preserve capitalization. The team therefore separated change visibility and exact-match semantics into another worksheet. A method can retrieve plausible descriptive passages quickly while violating either of those operational requirements. Deployment authors should combine the appropriate measurements only when they refer to the same build and index configuration, as they do throughout this packet.

x07s3 | Disconnected retrieval operations and index lifecycle review
The operations review used the same ordinary configurations and complete indices as the passage retrieval trial. The appliance was disconnected for seven days while replaying the query list and applying locally supplied changes. The team distinguished dependencies needed to build an index from those needed to continue querying it. A package that can answer several cached queries without a network is not necessarily suitable for an indefinitely disconnected installation, so the inspection also examined periodic entitlement and calibration behavior described by the shipped package."}
